```{r}
# Download R packages
library(tidyverse)
library(openxlsx)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)
library(extrafont)

# Make the Windows fonts available to the plots (Trebuchet MS, as in the text)
loadfonts(device = "win", quiet = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Income data: one row per contestant and income category (amounts in MDL and EUR)
# MM and BUN are left out, as in the figures of the digest
income_data <- read.xlsx("income_data.xlsx") %>%
  filter(!Competitor_Acronym %in% c("MM", "BUN")) %>%
  mutate(Income_Label = str_replace(Income_Label, "businesess", "businesses")) %>%
  group_by(Competitor_Acronym) %>%
  # total = net income (one contestant reported negative own funds), stack = sum of the positive items
  mutate(total_eur = sum(Amount_EUR),
         stack_eur = sum(Amount_EUR[Amount_EUR >= 0])) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(Competitor_Acronym = fct_reorder(Competitor_Acronym, total_eur))

# One row per contestant with total income
income_totals <- income_data %>%
  distinct(Competitor_Acronym, total_eur, stack_eur)

# Share of each income category in the income of each contestant (rows = contestants)
income_share <- income_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  mutate(share = Amount_EUR / sum(Amount_EUR), .by = Competitor_Acronym) %>%
  select(Competitor_Acronym, Income_Label, share) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Income_Label, values_from = share) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Competitor_Acronym")

# Share of each income category in the income of all contestants
category_share <- income_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  summarise(eur = sum(Amount_EUR), .by = Income_Label) %>%
  mutate(share = eur / sum(eur)) %>%
  select(Income_Label, share) %>%
  deframe()

# Four best-funded contestants versus the rest
top4 <- c("BEP", "PAS", "BEA", "PN")
total_all <- sum(income_totals$total_eur)
total_top4 <- income_totals %>% filter(Competitor_Acronym %in% top4) %>% pull(total_eur) %>% sum()

# Donations from businesses: who received them?
business <- income_data %>%
  filter(Income_Label == "Donations: businesses", Amount_EUR > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(Amount_EUR))

# Donor base: monetary donations and volunteer contributions (rows = contestants)
summary_donations <- read.xlsx("summary_donations.xlsx") %>%
  filter(party_acronym != "BUN")
summary_volunteers <- read.xlsx("summary_volunteers.xlsx")

don <- summary_donations %>% column_to_rownames("party_acronym")
vol <- summary_volunteers %>% column_to_rownames("party_acronym")
```

The parliamentary elections of 28 September 2025 in Moldova were held under stricter campaign finance rules. The changes adopted in June 2025 [@monitorul2025] followed evidence of large-scale illegal financing and foreign interference around the 2024 presidential election and the EU accession referendum. In this post, the first of a few based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest [@lipcean2026], I look at the *income side* of the campaign: how much money the contestants raised, where it came from, and how many contributions they received.

There is one caveat though. The analysis relies on the official financial reports that contestants filed with the Central Electoral Commission (CEC) through its online financial control platform [@cec2025financial]. It therefore says nothing about illicit or undeclared funding, which is by nature hard to measure. It can nevertheless show how legally declared resources are distributed, and that distribution is not equal.

***The rules of the game***

During this campaign, individuals could contribute up to six average monthly wages (AMW; MDL 96,600, about €4,950), while legal entities up to twelve AMW (MDL 193,200, about €9,900).[^1] Cash donations were capped at one AMW (MDL 16,100, about €825), businesses could donate only by bank transfer, companies with outstanding debts to the state budget or social security and health insurance funds were barred from donating, and contestants could not accept in-kind donations without advance payment [@monitorul2022]. Besides private money, contestants could move up to 70% of the state subsidies available in their party accounts into their election account.

[^1]: Throughout this post, amounts in euro are converted from lei at about MDL 19.5 per euro.

***Who raised the money?***

Collectively, the `r nrow(income_totals)` electoral contestants collected about `r dollar(total_all / 1e6, prefix = "€", accuracy = 0.1, suffix = " million")` of reported income. Panel A of Figure 1 shows that this money was extremely concentrated. The Patriotic Electoral Bloc (BEP) and the Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) each raised more than €1.2 million, followed by the Alternative Bloc (BEA) and Our Party (PN). These four contestants alone account for `r dollar(total_top4 / 1e6, prefix = "€", accuracy = 0.01, suffix = " million")`, or `r percent(total_top4 / total_all, accuracy = 1)` of the total, while the remaining `r nrow(income_totals) - length(top4)` contestants raised together `r dollar((total_all - total_top4) / 1e6, prefix = "€", accuracy = 0.01, suffix = " million")`. The best-funded bloc raised several hundred times more than the smallest contestants.

Figure 1 has two panels that show the same contestants in two ways. In panel A each bar is one contestant, ranked from the largest to the smallest, and its length shows the total money it raised in thousand euro, with the number at the end of the bar giving the total. The colours split each bar by income source, from volunteer work to donations from businesses. Panel B stretches every bar to 100%, so that we can compare the mix of sources of each contestant regardless of how much it raised: for instance, the dark purple part of a bar is the share of volunteer work in that contestant's income.

```{r}
#| label: fig-income
#| fig-cap: "Campaign income of electoral contestants in Moldova's 2025 parliamentary elections, by income source. Panel A shows absolute amounts (the label is the net total income), panel B the share of each source."
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked bar charts of campaign income by contestant. Panel A shows absolute amounts in thousand euro, with BEP and PAS above 1.2 million and most contestants below 100 thousand. Panel B shows the share of each income source."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 8

# Panel A: absolute amounts
absolute <- income_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Competitor_Acronym,
             y = Amount_EUR / 1000,
             fill = fct_rev(Income_Label))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(data = income_totals,
            aes(x = Competitor_Acronym,
                y = stack_eur / 1000,
                label = comma(total_eur / 1000, accuracy = 1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = -0.1, size = 3, family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1500, 300),
                     labels = comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Income sources", end = 0.9) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_light(base_family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(linetype = 3),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    legend.key.width = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.65, 0.25)
  ) +
  labs(title = "A: Absolute numbers", x = "", y = "€ thousand")

# Panel B: share of each source in the income of each contestant
relative <- income_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Competitor_Acronym,
             y = Amount_EUR,
             fill = fct_rev(Income_Label))) +
  geom_col(position = position_fill()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Income sources", end = 0.9) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_light(base_family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(linetype = 3),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  labs(title = "B: Percentage", x = "", y = "Percentage")

# Combine both panels
absolute + relative
```

## Acronyms of electoral contestants

```{r}
read.xlsx("acronims.xlsx") %>%
  rename(Acronym = party_acronym, `Electoral contestant` = party_name_en) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```
:::

***Where did the money come from?***

Panel B of Figure 1 shows that contestants also relied on very different sources of money. Volunteer work, valued by the contestants themselves, is the largest income source (`r percent(category_share[["Volunteer work"]], accuracy = 1)` of everything reported), followed by donations from individuals (`r percent(category_share[["Donations: individuals"]], accuracy = 1)`). Own funds, donations from businesses, in-kind donations and the state subsidies that parties moved to their campaign accounts each make up much smaller shares.[^2]

[^2]: The value of volunteer work is set by the contestant, using the AMW as a reference. It depends on the level of the electoral body the volunteer worked for: 50% for representatives at the Central Electoral Commission or in courts, 30% at second-level district councils, 20% at first-level district councils, and 10% at polling stations.

Behind these totals are different strategies. PAS, the party in government, used several sources at once: individual donations make up `r percent(income_share["PAS", "Donations: individuals"], accuracy = 1)` of its reported income, volunteer work `r percent(income_share["PAS", "Volunteer work"], accuracy = 1)`, its own funds `r percent(income_share["PAS", "Own private funds"], accuracy = 1)` and donations from businesses `r percent(income_share["PAS", "Donations: businesses"], accuracy = 1)`. BEP, by contrast, relied on volunteers for `r percent(income_share["BEP", "Volunteer work"], accuracy = 1)` of its income and received no business donations at all. BEA and PN relied mostly on individual donors (`r percent(income_share["BEA", "Donations: individuals"], accuracy = 1)` and `r percent(income_share["PN", "Donations: individuals"], accuracy = 1)`), plus volunteer work. Most smaller contestants depended on one or two sources, which left them financially vulnerable.

***Individual versus business money***

Business donations tell a different story from individual ones. Only two contestants collected large amounts from businesses: PAS (`r dollar(business$Amount_EUR[business$Competitor_Acronym == "PAS"], prefix = "€", accuracy = 1)`) and the Moldovans Alliance (AM, `r dollar(business$Amount_EUR[business$Competitor_Acronym == "AM"], prefix = "€", accuracy = 1)`). For PAS this is `r percent(income_share["PAS", "Donations: businesses"], accuracy = 1)` of its income, but for AM it is `r percent(income_share["AM", "Donations: businesses"], accuracy = 1)`, so AM depended much more on business money. All other contestants together raised only `r dollar(sum(business$Amount_EUR[!business$Competitor_Acronym %in% c("PAS", "AM")]), prefix = "€", accuracy = 1)` from businesses. Business money was therefore scarce, and went mostly to the party in government. A different question is whether some money declared as individual donations really comes from businesses or other interests. Journalists have raised this issue, and I discuss it in the digest [@lipcean2026].

***Many small donors or a few big ones?***

Totals do not show how contestants raised their money, so Figure 2 plots, for each contestant, the total amount raised (x-axis) against the number of contributions it received (y-axis). Both axes use a logarithmic scale, where each step is a multiplication, thus helping to fit small and large contestants in the same picture. The size and colour of each point show the average contribution: a big, light-coloured point means few but large contributions, while a small, dark point means many small ones. Panel A covers contributions in money and panel B volunteer contributions. In money donations (panel A), PAS has by far the most contributions, `r comma(don["PAS", "n_contributors"])`, with an average of only €`r round(don["PAS", "avg_contribution_eur"])`, the lowest of all contestants. This is what raising money from many small donors looks like. BEA (`r comma(don["BEA", "n_contributors"])` contributions, average €`r round(don["BEA", "avg_contribution_eur"])`) and PN (`r comma(don["PN", "n_contributors"])`, €`r round(don["PN", "avg_contribution_eur"])`) raised similar totals with larger average donations, while BEP collected only `r comma(don["BEP", "n_contributors"])` monetary contributions (average €`r round(don["BEP", "avg_contribution_eur"])`). At the other end, `r sum(summary_donations$n_contributors < 20)` of the `r nrow(summary_donations)` contestants reported fewer than 20 monetary contributions, and AM got only `r don["AM", "n_contributors"]`, averaging €`r comma(round(don["AM", "avg_contribution_eur"]))`.

Panel B shows even bigger gaps in volunteer work. BEP reported `r comma(vol["BEP", "n_contributors"])` volunteer contributions with a total value above €1 million, an average of only €`r round(vol["BEP", "avg_contribution_eur"])` each. PAS, the party in government, reported less than half as many (`r comma(vol["PAS", "n_contributors"])`), followed by PN (`r comma(vol["PN", "n_contributors"])`), MRM (`r comma(vol["MRM", "n_contributors"])`) and BEA (`r comma(vol["BEA", "n_contributors"])`). Most other contestants reported fewer than 100 contributions. So volunteers widen the gaps between contestants instead of closing them: well-funded contestants with strong organisations mobilised thousands of supporters, while those with little money did not reach even small groups of volunteers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-donors
#| fig-cap: "Donor networks of electoral contestants in Moldova's 2025 parliamentary elections: total amount raised and number of contributions (both on log scales). The size and colour of each point show the average contribution in euro."
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots with logarithmic axes. Each point is an electoral contestant, placed by total contributions in thousand euro and number of contributions. Panel A shows monetary contributions, panel B volunteer contributions."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 8

# Panel A: monetary contributions
monetary_donations <- summary_donations %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_funds_eur / 1000, y = n_contributors)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = avg_contribution_eur, colour = avg_contribution_eur)) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = party_acronym), colour = "grey30", size = 3, family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1500)) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 50, 200, 500, 1500)) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Average \ncontribution €",
                        breaks = seq(0, 3600, 600),
                        labels = comma,
                        range = c(2, 8)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Average \ncontribution €",
                         breaks = seq(0, 3600, 600),
                         labels = comma,
                         end = 0.9) +
  guides(size = guide_legend(), colour = guide_legend()) + # merge both legends
  labs(title = "A: Monetary contributions",
       x = "Total contributions: € thousands",
       y = "Number of contributions") +
  theme_light(base_family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.margin = margin(b = -0.5, unit = "lines"),
        legend.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(linetype = 3))

# Panel B: volunteer contributions
voluntary_donations <- summary_volunteers %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_funds_eur / 1000, y = n_contributors)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = avg_contribution_eur, colour = avg_contribution_eur)) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = party_acronym), colour = "grey30", size = 3, family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(5, 50, 500, 2500, 10000, 20000)) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Average \ncontribution €",
                        breaks = seq(0, 500, 75),
                        labels = comma,
                        range = c(2, 8)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Average \ncontribution €",
                         breaks = seq(0, 500, 75),
                         labels = comma,
                         end = 0.9) +
  guides(size = guide_legend(), colour = guide_legend()) +
  labs(title = "B: Volunteer contributions",
       x = "Total contributions: € thousands",
       y = "Number of contributions") +
  theme_light(base_family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.margin = margin(b = -0.5, unit = "lines"),
        legend.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(linetype = 3))

# Combine both panels
monetary_donations + voluntary_donations
```

***What this means for competition***

The playing field was very uneven. A small group of well-established contestants raised far more than everyone else, and they used several sources at the same time: individual donations, business money, their own funds and volunteers. Most of the others depended on one or two sources, usually small individual donations or a handful of volunteers. At the same time, the money was not concentrated in a single party. PAS, the party in government, was not the only one to raise large amounts: BEA, PN and BEP did too, and several contestants mobilised thousands of volunteers.

Did this money turn into votes? I come back to this in a later post, after looking at how contestants spent their money.
